claim: Hin is a member of the DNA invertase subclass of serine recombinases that are regulated by a remote recombinational enhancer element containing two binding sites for the protein Fis.
source: Hin is a member of the DNA invertase subclass of serine recombinases that are regulated by a remote recombinational enhancer element containing two binding sites for the protein Fis.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing Hin's classification and regulatory mechanism.

claim: Two Hin dimers bound to specific recombination sites associate with the Fis-bound enhancer by DNA looping where they are remodeled into a synaptic tetramer competent for DNA chemistry and exchange.
source: Two Hin dimers bound to specific recombination sites associate with the Fis-bound enhancer by DNA looping where they are remodeled into a synaptic tetramer competent for DNA chemistry and exchange.
evidence: This statement describes the mechanism of Hin recombination complex assembly.

claim: The flexible beta-hairpin arms of the Fis dimers contact the DNA binding domain of one subunit of each Hin dimer.
source: Here we show that the flexible beta-hairpin arms of the Fis dimers contact the DNA binding domain of one subunit of each Hin dimer.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by crosslinking experiments.

claim: The Fis-Hin contacts sandwich the Hin dimers to promote remodeling into the tetramer.
source: These contacts sandwich the Hin dimers to promote remodeling into the tetramer.
evidence: This describes the functional consequence of the Fis-Hin interactions.

claim: A basic region on the Hin catalytic domain contacts enhancer DNA to complete assembly of the active Hin tetramer.
source: A basic region on the Hin catalytic domain then contacts enhancer DNA to complete assembly of the active Hin tetramer.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by mutagenesis and FeBABE experiments.

claim: Hin inverts a ∼1 kb segment of chromosomal DNA between two 26 bp hix recombination sites in Salmonella enterica.
source: Hin inverts a ∼1 kb segment of chromosomal DNA between two 26 bp hix recombination sites in Salmonella enterica (Zieg et al., 1977; Zieg and Simon, 1980).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Inversion switches the orientation of a promoter, resulting in alternative expression of flagellin genes.
source: Inversion switches the orientation of a promoter, resulting in alternative expression of flagellin genes.
evidence: This describes the biological function of Hin-mediated DNA inversion.

claim: Flagellar phase variation is one way that Salmonella evades the host immune system.
source: Flagellar phase variation is one way that Salmonella evades the host immune system.
evidence: This describes the biological significance of the Hin system.

claim: The hin enhancer is normally positioned about 100 bp from one of the hix sites.
source: Whereas the hin enhancer is normally positioned about 100 bp from one of the hix sites, it can efficiently activate DNA inversion many kb away from the closest hix site by DNA looping (Johnson and Simon, 1985; Kahmann et al., 1985).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The hin enhancer can efficiently activate DNA inversion many kb away from the closest hix site by DNA looping.
source: Whereas the hin enhancer is normally positioned about 100 bp from one of the hix sites, it can efficiently activate DNA inversion many kb away from the closest hix site by DNA looping (Johnson and Simon, 1985; Kahmann et al., 1985).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Wild-type Hin is chemically inactive without the Fis/enhancer system.
source: Whereas wild-type Hin is chemically inactive without the Fis/enhancer system, mutants that no longer require the Fis/enhancer element or DNA supercoiling have been isolated (Klippel et al., 1988; Sanders and Johnson, 2004; Heiss et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hyperactive Hin mutants catalyze recombination promiscuously, being no longer restricted to promoting inversion between recombination sites on the same DNA molecule and no longer confined to a single round of subunit rotation.
source: These hyperactive mutants catalyze recombination promiscuously, being no longer restricted to promoting inversion between recombination sites on the same DNA molecule and no longer confined to a single round of subunit rotation.
evidence: This describes the properties of hyperactive Hin mutants.

claim: Three residues on one of the mobile β-hairpin arms of the Fis dimer are required to activate Hin-catalyzed DNA inversion through direct contact with Hin.
source: Three residues on one of the mobile β-hairpin arms of the Fis dimer are required to activate Hin-catalyzed DNA inversion through direct contact with Hin (Figure 1B) (Koch et al., 1991; Osuna et al., 1991; Safo et al., 1997; Dhar et al., 2009a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Fis-Q21C exhibits efficient crosslinking with Hin using AMAS crosslinker.
source: Crosslinking of Fis-Q21C to a lysine on Hin generates a radiolabeled Fis-Hin-DNA product, in addition to the covalently-linked Hin-DNA product from cleaved invertasomes (Figure 2C, Hin-wt panel; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Hin-K51A and K158A exhibited reduced amounts of Fis-Hin-(32P-DNA) crosslinked products relative to Hin-wt.
source: Hin-K51A and K158A exhibited reduced amounts of Fis-Hin-(32P-DNA) crosslinked products relative to Hin-wt (Figure 2B,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Hin-K146C at the N-terminus of helix 1 within the DBD generated ∼15% crosslinked Fis-Hin products using BMOE.
source: Hin-K146C at the N-terminus of helix 1 within the DBD generated ∼15% crosslinked Fis-Hin products (Figure 2B,D), a level similar to that of wild-type Hin crosslinked to Fis-Q21C by AMAS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: Hin-H147C, Hin-E150C, and Hin-Q151C within the α-helix formed crosslinks with Fis-Q21C using BMOE.
source: Hin-H147C, Hin-E150C, and Hin-Q151C within the α-helix formed crosslinks with Fis-Q21C, but H160C in the loop connecting to DBD helix 2 did not generate crosslinks.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Hin-L155A exhibits a >50-fold decrease of Fis-activated DNA inversion rates in vitro.
source: The most severe mutant, Hin-L155A, exhibits a >50-fold decrease of Fis-activated DNA inversion rates in vitro, comparable to the effects of the strongest Fis β-hairpin arm point mutations (Safo et al., 1997) (see also Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hin-H107Y/L155A catalyzes recombination in the absence of Fis at similar rates to Hin-H107Y.
source: In contrast, both Hin-H107Y and the double mutant Hin-H107Y/L155A catalyze recombination in the absence of Fis at similar rates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Fis contacts the DBDs of only the bottom two Hin subunits within the cleaved invertasome.
source: These crosslinking results demonstrate that Fis contacts the DBDs of only the bottom two Hin subunits within the cleaved invertasome as drawn in Figure 3A.
evidence: This is supported by crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Fis-Hin crosslinks only occurred with Hin subunits bound to hix1L and hix2R.
source: Fis-Hin crosslinks were only observed when Hin was bound to hix1L or to hix2R; no Fis-Hin crosslinks formed at hix1R or hix2L.
evidence: This is supported by crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The combinations of K47A/R48A and R48A/K51A severely impair Fis-activated Hin inversion both in vivo and in vitro.
source: However, the combinations of K47A/R48A and R48A/K51A severely impair Fis-activated Hin inversion both in vivo and in vitro (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Hin-R48A/K51A/H107Y promotes Fis-independent inversion at rates that are indistinguishable from the single H107Y mutant.
source: Hin-R48A/K51A/H107Y promotes Fis-independent inversion at rates that are indistinguishable from the single H107Y mutant (Figure 4C), demonstrating that these mutations are not disturbing Hin catalytic properties.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Hin-R48A and Hin-K51A are insensitive to the length of the loop between the hix1 site and the enhancer in knotting experiments.
source: Hin-R48A and Hin-K51A, however, are insensitive to the length of the loop between the hix1 site and the enhancer; both mutants knotted about 40% of the reacted short spacer substrates corresponding to an eightfold increase in processive DNA exchange compared with wild-type Hin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Hin-N54C-FeBABE generated two prominent scission sites within the center of the enhancer segment.
source: Hin-N54C-FeBABE, and to a lesser extent Hin-Y52C-FeBABE, generated two prominent scission sites within the center of the enhancer segment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The scission sites by Hin-N54C-FeBABE are located between the Fis dimer binding sites.
source: These are located between the Fis dimer binding sites, as demarked by DNA scission induced by Fis-N98C coupled with FeBABE (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B); DNA scission by chemical nucleases coupled to Fis residue 98 has been used previously to map Fis binding site locations (Pan et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and citation to previous work.

claim: When most of the DNA between the two Fis binding sites is replaced by non-native sequence, Hin inversion rates are reduced about fivefold.
source: When most of the DNA between the two Fis binding sites is replaced by non-native sequence (pRJ765, Figure 5D), Hin inversion rates are reduced about fivefold (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: When only the two A/T-rich segments identified to be in proximity to the Hin helix-B region are replaced by G/C-rich sequences, Hin inversion rates are reduced 2.5-fold.
source: When only the two A/T-rich segments identified to be in proximity to the Hin helix-B region by the FeBABE experiments are replaced by G/C-rich sequences (pRJ2943, Figure 5D), Hin inversion rates are reduced 2.5-fold (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Hin dimers that are covalently crosslinked with Fis on the enhancer can be remodeled into catalytically-active tetramers.
source: We conclude that Hin dimers that are covalently crosslinked with Fis on the enhancer can be remodeled into catalytically-active tetramers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Ligation can efficiently occur when Hin is covalently linked to Fis.
source: We conclude that ligation can efficiently occur when Hin is covalently linked to Fis, reinforcing earlier topological data indicating that the enhancer normally remains associated with the Hin complex throughout the reaction (Heichman et al., 1991; Merickel and Johnson, 2004; Dhar et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and citations to previous work.

claim: The hin enhancer contains two Fis dimer binding sites separated by 47 bp between their centers.
source: The hin enhancer contains two Fis dimer binding sites separated by 47 bp between their centers (Figure 5D) (Johnson and Simon, 1985; Bruist et al., 1987; Johnson et al., 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work and reference to Figure 5D.

claim: Hin residues Arg154, Leu155, and Gln151 are conserved among Fis/enhancer-dependent DNA invertases, but not the related resolvases.
source: Significantly, Hin residues Arg154, Leu155, and Gln151, which also may contribute to the Fis contact patch, are conserved among Fis/enhancer-dependent DNA invertases, but not the related resolvases (Figure 8A), further supporting the function of these residues in the Fis-activation step.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The basic character of key residues within the helix-B region is uniquely conserved among the DNA invertase subclass of serine recombinases.
source: The basic character of key residues within the helix-B region is also uniquely conserved among the DNA invertase subclass of serine recombinases (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Of the 15 DNA invertases aligned, residue 47 is always a lysine, and residues 48 and 51 are equally represented by lysine and arginine.
source: Of the 15 DNA invertases we have aligned, residue 47 is always a lysine, and residues 48 and 51 are equally represented by lysine and arginine, suggesting they are not involved in base-specific interactions.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Members of the resolvase or integrase subclasses of serine recombinases tend to not have lysines and arginines at the same positions as DNA invertases in the helix-B region.
source: Members of the resolvase or integrase subclasses of serine recombinases, which are not regulated by a Fis/enhancer system, tend to not have lysines and arginines at the same positions, and the electrostatic surface over this region in the resolvase tetramer is much less basic (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment and structural comparison data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Fis/enhancer system initially functions to promote synapsis and remodeling of Hin dimers into the active tetramer.
source: However, the Fis/enhancer system initially functions much earlier in the pathway to promote synapsis and remodeling of Hin dimers into the active tetramer, as wild-type Hin is unable to form active tetramers without the Fis/enhancer element (Dhar et al., 2004; Sanders and Johnson, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Fis is able to productively contact inactive Hin dimers.
source: We demonstrate here that Fis is able to productively contact inactive Hin dimers and that Hin dimers covalently crosslinked to Fis can transition into an active tetramer competent for DNA cleavage (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: A single clockwise rotation of subunits together with their linked DNA strands will result in inversion of the DNA between the hix sites with an accompanying loss of four supercoils.
source: A single clockwise rotation of subunits together with their linked DNA strands will result in inversion of the DNA between the hix sites with an accompanying loss of four supercoils, as shown for Hin- and Gin-mediated DNA inversion (Kanaar et al., 1988; Merickel and Johnson, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The multiple connections stabilizing the Hin tetramer onto the Fis/enhancer element function to restrict processive subunit exchanges.
source: Thus, the multiple connections stabilizing the Hin tetramer onto the Fis/enhancer element function to restrict processive subunit exchanges.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased knotting with mutants that destabilize enhancer interactions.

claim: The invertasome normally remains intact over the course of the entire reaction.
source: We experimentally demonstrate in this work that the final chemical step in the reaction, Hin-catalyzed DNA ligation, can efficiently occur when Fis and Hin remain physically connected (Figure 6F), implying that the invertasome normally remains intact over the course of the entire reaction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Serine recombinases are often tightly controlled by elaborate, topologically-defined, nucleoprotein complexes.
source: Serine recombinases are often tightly controlled by elaborate, topologically-defined, nucleoprotein complexes.
evidence: This is a general statement about serine recombinases based on established knowledge.

claim: All four DNA strands are cleaved by near simultaneous attack on the DNA backbone by the catalytic serines to form 5′-phosphoserine linkages, thereby generating double-strand breaks at both recombination sites.
source: All four DNA strands are cleaved by near simultaneous attack on the DNA backbone by the catalytic serines to form 5′-phosphoserine linkages, thereby generating double-strand breaks at both recombination sites.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of DNA cleavage by serine recombinases.

claim: DNA strands are exchanged by a subunit rotation mechanism where one pair of synapsed subunits, together with their covalently-bound DNA strands, rotates 180° relative to the other pair.
source: DNA strands are then exchanged by a subunit rotation mechanism where one pair of synapsed subunits, together with their covalently-bound DNA strands, rotates 180° relative to the other pair (Stark et al., 1989; Dhar et al., 2004, 2009a, 2009b; Li et al., 2005; Bai et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The synaptic complexes formed by serine recombinases contain the two recombining DNA segments on the outside of a tetrameric protein core.
source: The synaptic complexes formed by serine recombinases contain the two recombining DNA segments on the outside of a tetrameric protein core (Dhar et al., 2004; Nollmann et al., 2004; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Most site-specific recombinases can be classified into two structurally and mechanistically unrelated groups that are named for the use of either a serine or tyrosine as the active site residue.
source: Most site-specific recombinases can be classified into two structurally and mechanistically unrelated groups that are named for the use of either a serine or tyrosine as the active site residue (Grindley et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Site-specific recombination reactions have evolved as a relatively simple solution to a myriad of biological problems including gene regulation, viral integration, DNA transposition, chromosome segregation, and the programmed creation of genetic diversity.
source: Site-specific recombination reactions have evolved as a relatively simple solution to a myriad of biological problems including gene regulation, viral integration, DNA transposition, chromosome segregation, and the programmed creation of genetic diversity (Craig, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The primary interaction surface between Fis and Hin is composed of Val16 and Val22 on Fis and Leu155 on Hin together with Asp20 on Fis and Arg154 on Hin.
source: Our data are consistent with the primary interaction surface between these proteins being composed of Val16 and Val22 on Fis and Leu155 on Hin together with Asp20 on Fis and Arg154 on Hin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from mutagenesis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Attractive electrostatic forces between the helix-B region and the enhancer DNA promote the final conformational change into the active tetramer structure.
source: Finally, attractive electrostatic forces between the helix-B region and the enhancer DNA promote the final conformational change into the active tetramer structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural model and experimental data.

claim: Conformational energy from the Fis/enhancer segment may be harvested to drive tetramer assembly forward.
source: Conformational energy from the Fis/enhancer segment may also be harvested to drive tetramer assembly forward.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of tetramer assembly.

claim: The supercoiling energy in the looped DNA between the enhancer and hix sites drives the clockwise rotation of the top pair of subunits relative to the static bottom subunit pair that is fixed onto the enhancer.
source: In our invertasome model the supercoiling energy in the looped DNA between the enhancer and hix sites drives the clockwise rotation of the top pair of subunits relative to the static bottom subunit pair that is fixed onto the enhancer (Figure 7D,E; Video 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural model.

claim: The small loop between the enhancer and hix site will inhibit additional subunit rotations because of torsional strain generated from multiple DNA windings.
source: When the distance between a hix site and the enhancer is short, as in the native configuration in the Salmonella chromosome (∼100 bp between hixL and the proximal Fis binding site), the small loop will inhibit additional subunit rotations because of torsional strain generated from multiple DNA windings (illustrated in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an inference based on topological considerations.

claim: For Sin the interaction between regulatory and catalytic subunits involves residues Phe52 and Arg54 that are located immediately adjacent to helix-B.
source: For Sin this interaction involves residues Phe52 and Arg54 that are located immediately adjacent to helix-B (Figure 8B) (Mouw et al., 2008; Rowland et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work and reference to Figure 8B.

claim: For γδ/Tn3 resolvases a cluster of residues (Arg2, Arg32, Lys54, and Glu56) comprising the so-called 2–3′ interface between regulatory and catalytic dimers is important for assembly of the active synaptosome.
source: For γδ/Tn3 resolvases a cluster of residues (Arg2, Arg32, Lys54, and Glu56; Figure 8B) comprising the so-called 2–3′ interface between regulatory and catalytic dimers is important for assembly of the active synaptosome (Hughes et al., 1990; Murley and Grindley, 1998; Burke et al., 2004; Olorunniji et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work and reference to Figure 8B.

claim: The interaction between regulatory and catalytic subunits in the resolvase reactions is dispensable in the context of strong hyperactive mutants that promote indiscriminant recombination.
source: Like Hin, the interaction between regulatory and catalytic subunits in the resolvase reactions is dispensable in the context of strong hyperactive mutants that promote indiscriminant recombination (Burke et al., 2004; Olorunniji et al., 2008; Rowland et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Protein-protein or DNA-protein forces acting on the helix-B region may not only stabilize the active recombination complex but promote remodeling of this subfamily of serine recombinases into their active tetrameric conformation.
source: Taken together, the Hin, Sin, and γδ/Tn3 results imply that protein-protein or DNA-protein forces acting on this region of the catalytic domain may not only stabilize the active recombination complex but promote remodeling of this subfamily of serine recombinases into their active tetrameric conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of data from multiple systems.
